mainTopic: Torah study above the תמיד, an angel's defense of Israel, praying ahead of trouble, עכן's atonement, a condemned man's claim of innocence, and the start of the stoning procedure
overview: This amud finishes the story of the angel who met יהושע. The angel says יהושע's people neglected the afternoon תמיד and also תלמוד תורה. From the angel's words 'I have come now,' רב learns that תלמוד תורה is greater than bringing the תמידין. Next, אביי asks רב דימי how ארץ ישראל explains a פסוק in משלי. רב דימי answers with the story of an angel who protested when יחזקאל was told to shame Israel's ancestors, and the גמרא explains that angel's three names. Three אמוראים then explain a פסוק in איוב about praying before trouble comes. The גמרא returns to the משנה and proves that עכן's confession earned him a share in עולם הבא, and that he is the same man as זמרי. It then explains why a condemned man may not declare his innocence, and tells of a man who did, whose sentence still stood even when the witnesses took back their testimony. Finally a new משנה begins about removing the clothes of the person being stoned.

steps.title: The angel tells יהושע what was neglected
steps.stepSummary: The angel tells יהושע that yesterday they missed the afternoon תמיד, and now they are missing תלמוד תורה.
steps.simpleTranslation: The angel said to יהושע: Yesterday you neglected the afternoon daily offering, and now you are neglecting Torah study.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא continues the story of the angel who appeared to יהושע. The angel names two things the people neglected because of the war.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Two failures are listed. The first is the afternoon תמיד, which was missed yesterday while they were fighting. The second is תלמוד תורה, which is being missed right now, at night. This sets up the question of which failure is worse.

phrases.english: He said to him: Yesterday you neglected
phrases.notes: The angel is the one speaking here, and he is talking to יהושע.

phrases.english: the daily afternoon offering,
and now you have neglected Torah study.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the story of the angel's appearance to יהושע, which began before this section.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The angel rebukes יהושע for neglecting both the תמיד and תלמוד תורה.

steps.title: יהושע asks which failure the angel came about
steps.stepSummary: יהושע asks which of the two neglected things brought the angel.
steps.simpleTranslation: For which of them have you come?
steps.whatsHappening: יהושע asks a question so he will know what to fix first. This sets up the angel's answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: יהושע wants to know which neglect is the main problem. The answer will show which of the two is more serious.

phrases.english: For which of them have you come?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Responds to the angel's two complaints by asking which one is the main one.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which neglect, the תמיד or תלמוד תורה, caused the angel to come.

steps.title: The angel answers: I have come now
steps.stepSummary: The angel answers with the words of the פסוק, 'I have come now,' showing he came about the missed learning.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: 'I have now come.'
steps.whatsHappening: The angel answers יהושע using the words of the פסוק. 'Now' means at this moment, at night, when they are not learning.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the angel had come about the תמיד, he would have come yesterday afternoon. Since he came now, at night, the missed תלמוד תורה is what brought him. That shows it is the more serious failure.
steps.confusionAlert: 'Now' is not just a filler word. The whole point rests on it: the angel came now, during the time of missed learning, and not yesterday, during the time of the missed offering.

phrases.english: He said to him: "I have now come."
phrases.notes: These are the angel's words in יהושע 5:14.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers יהושע's question.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The angel came because of the neglected תלמוד תורה, as shown by the word 'now'.

steps.title: יהושע spends the night deep in הלכה
steps.stepSummary: יהושע immediately fixed the problem. רבי יוחנן reads 'he lodged in the valley' as 'he spent the night in the depth of הלכה.'
steps.simpleTranslation: Immediately, 'And יהושע lodged that night in the midst of the valley.' And רבי יוחנן said: This teaches that he spent the night in the depth of הלכה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows that יהושע fixed the problem right away. It uses a פסוק that רבי יוחנן reads as a hint to Torah learning.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word עמק (valley) sounds like עומק (depth). So רבי יוחנן reads the פסוק as saying יהושע spent the whole night deep in learning הלכה. This makes up for the learning that was missed.

keyTerms.meaning: And he lodged, he spent the night

phrases.english: Immediately, "And Joshua lodged
phrases.notes: The quote mixes two פסוקים: יהושע 8:9 and 8:13.

phrases.english: that night in the midst of the valley,"
and Rabbi Yoḥanan said:
This teaches that he lodged in the depth of halakha.
phrases.notes: This is a wordplay: עמק (valley) is read like עומק (depth).

steps.triggerLanguage: מִיָּד וַיָּלֶן יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בַּלַּיְלָה הַהוּא בְּתוֹךְ הָעֵמֶק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows יהושע's response to the angel's answer.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: יהושע fixed the missed learning by spending the night deeply learning הלכה.

steps.title: Torah study is greater than bringing the daily offerings
steps.stepSummary: רב, quoted by שמואל בר אינייא, concludes from 'I have now come' that תלמוד תורה is greater than bringing the תמידין.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל בר אינייא said in the name of רב: Torah study is greater than bringing the daily offerings, as it says, 'I have now come.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא states the lesson of the whole story. Learning Torah is greater than bringing the daily offerings.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proof is the angel's word 'now.' The angel came about the missed learning, not the missed offering. So neglecting learning is the more serious failure, which means learning is the greater מצוה.
steps.whatToRemember: The angel came 'now,' at night, about the missed learning. From this, רב learns that תלמוד תורה is greater than bringing the תמידין.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is a well-known source for how important תלמוד תורה is, even compared with the daily service in the מקדש.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר אִינְיָא מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרַב:
phrases.english: Shmuel bar Unya said in the name of Rav:
Torah study is greater
than the sacrificing of the daily offerings,
as it is stated: "I have now come."

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר אִינְיָא מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the general lesson from the angel's answer.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: תלמוד תורה is greater than bringing the תמידין, as shown by the angel's words 'I have now come.'

steps.title: אביי asks how ארץ ישראל explains a פסוק in משלי
steps.stepSummary: אביי asks רב דימי how the scholars in ארץ ישראל explain the פסוק 'Do not go out hastily to fight.'
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said to רב דימי: How do you in the West explain this פסוק: 'Do not go out hastily to fight, lest you not know what to do at the end of it, when your neighbor shames you. Argue your case with your neighbor, and do not reveal another's secret'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic. אביי asks how the scholars in ארץ ישראל explain a פסוק in משלי, and this question sets up the answer that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Nothing is being decided yet. אביי is asking for the ארץ ישראל reading of the פסוק. The next step gives רב דימי's answer.

keyTerms.meaning: In the West, meaning ארץ ישראל
How do you explain it? Literally, 'in what do you set it?'
To a fight or a court case

phrases.english: Abaye said to Rav Dimi:
This verse, in the West,
phrases.notes: 'The West' means ארץ ישראל, where רב דימי came from.

phrases.english: how do you explain it:
"Do not go out hastily to litigation,
phrases.notes: משלי 25:8–9

phrases.english: lest you know not what to do in the end of it,
when your neighbor has put you to shame.
Debate your cause with your neighbor,
and do not reveal the secret of another"?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ אַבָּיֵי לְרַב דִּימִי הַאי קְרָא בְּמַעְרְבָא בְּמַאי מוֹקְמִיתוּ לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic after the story of יהושע and the angel ends.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How the scholars of ארץ ישראל explain the פסוק in משלי 25:8–9.

steps.title: The angel protests on behalf of אברהם and שרה
steps.stepSummary: רב דימי answers אביי: when הקב״ה told יחזקאל to call Israel the children of an Amorite and a Hittite, an angel protested that this would shame אברהם and שרה.
steps.simpleTranslation: When הקב״ה told יחזקאל to tell Israel, 'Your father was an Amorite and your mother a Hittite,' the angel רוח פסקונית said: Master of the world, if אברהם and שרה came and stood before You, would You say this to their faces and shame them? The פסוק says, 'Debate your cause with your neighbor, and do not reveal the secret of another.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב דימי gives the answer to אביי's question by telling a story about an angel who defended the honor of Israel's ancestors.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The angel quotes the next פסוק in משלי, 'Debate your cause with your neighbor.' He means: argue with Israel about their own sins, but do not expose the shame of their ancestors. So the pair of פסוקים is read as advice given to God about how to rebuke Israel.

keyTerms.meaning: An angel; the name comes from 'cutting' or interrupting words
Debate your cause with your neighbor
Do not reveal another person's secret

phrases.aramaic: בְּשָׁעָה שֶׁאָמַר לוֹ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לִיחֶזְקֵאל:
phrases.english: At the time that the Holy One, Blessed be He, said to Ezekiel:
Go say to Israel
"Your father was an Amorite and your mother a Hittite,"
phrases.notes: יחזקאל 16:3

phrases.aramaic: אָמְרָה רוּחַ פִּסְקוֹנִית לִפְנֵי הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא:
phrases.english: the spirit Piskonit said before the Holy One, Blessed be He:
phrases.notes: This is an angel. The גמרא explains his name in a moment.

phrases.english: Master of the Universe,

phrases.aramaic: אִם יָבוֹאוּ אַבְרָהָם וְשָׂרָה וְיַעַמְדוּ לְפָנֶיךָ,
phrases.english: if Abraham and Sarah would come and stand before You,
would You say this to them and put them to shame?
"Debate your cause with your neighbor,
and do not reveal the secret of another"!
phrases.notes: משלי 25:9. It is the very next פסוק after 'Do not go out hastily to fight.'

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּשָׁעָה שֶׁאָמַר לוֹ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לִיחֶזְקֵאל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers אביי's question about how the scholars of ארץ ישראל read the פסוק in משלי.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The פסוקים are read as an angel's plea not to shame Israel by exposing their ancestors' lowly origins.

steps.title: How could an angel speak so boldly to God?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether an angel really has the authority to challenge הקב״ה like this.
steps.simpleTranslation: Does this angel really have that much permission?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is surprised by the story and asks how an angel could argue with God. This question sets up the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The story seems to show an angel correcting God, which is hard to accept. The question asks for a source showing that this angel has a special role that allows him to do this.

phrases.aramaic: וּמִי אִית לֵיהּ רְשׁוּתָא כּוּלֵּי הַאי?
phrases.english: But does he have so much authority?

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמִי אִית לֵיהּ רְשׁוּתָא כּוּלֵּי הַאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions how the story in step 7 is possible.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether, and why, this angel is allowed to argue with God.

steps.title: The angel's three names show his special role
steps.stepSummary: Yes. רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא teaches that the angel has three names, and each one describes how he defends Israel.
steps.simpleTranslation: Yes. רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא said: he has three names: פיסקון, איטמון, סיגרון. He is called פיסקון because he 'cuts' words toward Heaven. He is called איטמון because he seals up Israel's sins. He is called סיגרון because once he closes a matter, it is never opened again.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers yes and brings a teaching about the angel's three names to prove that his job is to argue for Israel.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each name is built on a Hebrew root: פסק means to cut or speak sharply, אטם means to seal shut, and סגר means to close. Together they show that boldly defending Israel before God is exactly his role.

keyTerms.meaning: From פסק, one who 'cuts' words and argues toward Heaven
From אטם, one who seals up and hides Israel's sins
From סגר, one who closes a matter for good

phrases.english: Yes,
as Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Ḥanina, said:
He has three names:
Piskon, Itmon, and Sigron.
Piskon, because he cuts words toward Above,
phrases.notes: He means the angel speaks sharply and argues with God.

phrases.english: Itmon, because he seals up the sins of Israel,
Sigron, because once he closes,
it is not opened again.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִין, דְּאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹסֵי בְּרַבִּי חֲנִינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 8.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Yes. The angel's three names show that his role is to argue for Israel before God.

steps.title: Pray before trouble comes, as אברהם did
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר reads the פסוק in איוב as teaching that a person should pray before trouble arrives, as אברהם did between בית אל and העי.
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק says, 'Had you prepared your prayer before trouble.' רבי אלעזר said: a person should always pray before trouble comes. If אברהם had not prayed ahead of time between בית אל and העי, nothing would have been left of Israel.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic: a teaching of רבי אלעזר about praying ahead of time, based on a פסוק in איוב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אברהם prayed at the place near העי long before Israel suffered a defeat there in the days of יהושע. רבי אלעזר says that earlier prayer is what saved Israel from being wiped out.

phrases.english: "Had you prepared your prayer before trouble came,"
phrases.notes: איוב 36:19

phrases.english: Rabbi Elazar said:
A person should always offer prayer before trouble comes,

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁאִילְמָלֵא לֹא הִקְדִּים אַבְרָהָם תְּפִלָּה לַצָּרָה
phrases.english: for had Abraham not offered prayer before the trouble
between Beit El and Ai,
there would not have remained of the enemies of Israel
phrases.notes: This is a polite way of saying Israel itself, so as not to speak of bad things happening to Israel.

phrases.english: a survivor or refugee.

steps.triggerLanguage: הֲיַעֲרֹךְ שׁוּעֲךָ לֹא בְצָר, אָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new אגדה teaching connected to the defeat at העי.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A person should always pray before trouble arrives.

steps.title: ריש לקיש: strong prayer below means no enemies above
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש reads the same פסוק differently: whoever puts effort into prayer down here will have no enemies in Heaven.
steps.simpleTranslation: ריש לקיש said: whoever strengthens himself in prayer down below will have no enemies up above.
steps.whatsHappening: ריש לקיש gives a second way to read the פסוק in איוב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He reads צר as 'enemy' instead of 'trouble.' So the פסוק means that someone who works hard at prayer will have no accusers against him in Heaven.

phrases.english: Reish Lakish said:
Whoever strengthens himself in prayer below,
has no enemies above.
phrases.notes: He reads the word צר in the פסוק as 'enemy' instead of 'trouble.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different reading of the same פסוק.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Effort in prayer below prevents enemies above.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן: pray that all will strengthen you
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן gives a third reading: a person should pray that everyone strengthens his power and that he has no enemies above.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said: a person should always ask for mercy that everyone will strengthen his power, and that he will have no enemies above.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן gives a third reading of the same פסוק and finishes this short section on prayer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Unlike ריש לקיש, who says that the person's own effort helps, רבי יוחנן says the person should pray for help from all others in strengthening him. The goal is the same: to have no adversaries in Heaven.

keyTerms.meaning: Should ask for mercy, should pray

phrases.english: Rabbi Yoḥanan said:
A person should always ask for mercy
that all should strengthen his power,
and that he should have no enemies above.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A third reading of the פסוק, close to ריש לקיש's reading.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Pray that all will strengthen you, so that you have no enemies above.

steps.title: Where do we see that עכן's confession atoned for him?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא returns to the משנה's question and brings a ברייתא that asks the same thing: what is the source that עכן's confession earned him atonement?
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'From where do we know that his confession atoned for him?' The Rabbis taught: From where do we know that his confession atoned for him?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the line of the משנה about עכן and brings a ברייתא that asks the same question. This sets up the proofs that follow.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה asked this question about עכן's confession. The ברייתא repeats the question so that it can give a full answer from פסוקים.

phrases.english: "From where do we know that his confession atoned for him, etc.?"
phrases.notes: This quotes the משנה, which is talking about עכן.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
From where do we know that his confession atoned for him?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the topic of prayer and returns to the משנה about עכן.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A source showing that עכן's confession brought him atonement.

steps.title: 'This day' you are troubled, but not in the next world
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא proves it from יהושע's words: 'God will trouble you this day.' Only today, but not in עולם הבא.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it says: 'And יהושע said to him: Why have you troubled us? God will trouble you this day.' This day you are troubled, but you will not be troubled in עולם הבא.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא brings its first proof, from what יהושע said to עכן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The extra words 'this day' are read as a limit. עכן's punishment happens only today, in this world. That shows his confession saved him in עולם הבא.

phrases.english: As it is stated:
"And Joshua said to him: Why have you brought trouble on us?
The Lord shall trouble you this day."
phrases.notes: יהושע 7:25

phrases.english: This day you are troubled,
but you are not troubled in the World-to-Come.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the first answer to the question of step 13.
steps.raayaObject: That עכן's confession atoned for him.
steps.raayaSupportSource: יהושע 7:25: 'this day' limits his punishment to this world.

steps.title: 'All five' have a share in עולם הבא
steps.stepSummary: A second proof: the פסוק lists the five sons of זרח, including זמרי, and says 'all five,' which teaches that all five have a share in עולם הבא.
steps.simpleTranslation: And it is written: 'The sons of זרח: זמרי, איתן, הימן, כלכל and דרדע, five in all.' Why does it say 'five in all'? To teach that all five of them have a share in עולם הבא.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא brings a second proof, from a list of names in דברי הימים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'five in all' seem extra, since we can count the names ourselves. So they teach that all five are equal in having a share in עולם הבא. Since זמרי here is understood to be עכן, this proves that his confession worked.

keyTerms.meaning: A son of זרח, understood here as עכן

steps.whatToRemember: עכן confessed before he died, and two פסוקים show that this earned him a share in עולם הבא: 'this day' limits his punishment to this world, and 'all five' includes him with his brothers.

phrases.english: And it is written:
"And the sons of Zerah: Zimri and Ethan and Heman
and Calcol and Dara, five of them in all."
phrases.notes: דברי הימים א 2:6. The גמרא takes זמרי here to be עכן and explains why soon.

phrases.english: What does "five of them in all" teach?
All five of them are destined for the World-to-Come.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second proof to the one in step 14.
steps.raayaObject: That עכן (זמרי) has a share in עולם הבא, so his confession atoned for him.
steps.raayaSupportSource: דברי הימים א 2:6: the seemingly extra words 'five of them in all.'

steps.title: Two different names in two different פסוקים
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא points out that one פסוק lists the son of זרח as זמרי, while another פסוק calls the sinner עכן.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is written 'זמרי,' and it is written 'עכן.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא notices that the list of זרח's sons says זמרי, but the story in יהושע calls the sinner עכן. It is setting up the next move, which explains how both names fit.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 15 used the list of זרח's five sons to prove that עכן has a share in עולם הבא. But that list never mentions עכן; it says זמרי. So the proof only works if זמרי and עכן are the same person, and the גמרא now has to explain the two names.

keyTerms.meaning: The name listed among the sons of זרח
The man who took from the forbidden spoils of יריחו

phrases.english: It is written "Zimri,"
phrases.notes: דברי הימים א 2:6

phrases.english: and it is written "Achan."
phrases.notes: יהושע 7:24

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Raises the name difference that the proof in step 15 depends on.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How can the פסוק listing זמרי be talking about עכן?

steps.title: First view: his real name was עכן
steps.stepSummary: רב and שמואל both say it is one person. One of them says his real name was עכן, and he was called זמרי because he acted like זמרי.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב and שמואל: One says his name was עכן. Why was he called זמרי? Because he did what זמרי did.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that זמרי and עכן are the same man. The first opinion says עכן was his real name, and זמרי was a nickname.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both רב and שמואל agree there is only one person, so the proof in step 15 stands. This opinion says the name זמרי was given to describe his behavior, comparing it to the famous sin of זמרי.

keyTerms.meaning: He was called by the name

phrases.english: Rav and Shmuel [disagree]:
One says: His name was Achan,
and why was he called Zimri?
Because he did the act of Zimri.
phrases.notes: This points to the זמרי of במדבר 25.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב וּשְׁמוּאֵל: חַד אָמַר, עָכָן שְׁמוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the name question from step 16.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: They are one person; his real name was עכן, and זמרי describes his deeds.

steps.title: Second view: his real name was זמרי
steps.stepSummary: The other opinion says his real name was זמרי, and he was called עכן because he brought on the sins of ישראל.
steps.simpleTranslation: And one says his name was זמרי. Why was he called עכן? Because he 'עיכן,' brought on the sins of ישראל.
steps.whatsHappening: The second opinion flips it: זמרי was the real name, and עכן was the nickname.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the name עכן is explained as a play on the word עיכן, describing how his sin brought punishment on all of ישראל. Either way, both opinions agree it is one man, so the proof that he has a share in עולם הבא holds.

keyTerms.meaning: That he 'coiled' or brought on (a wordplay on עכן)

steps.whatToRemember: רב and שמואל agree זמרי and עכן are the same person; they only argue which name was his real one.

phrases.english: And one says: His name was Zimri,
and why was he called Achan?
Because he brought on the sins of the Jewish people.
phrases.notes: עיכן sounds like עכן, as if he wrapped ישראל in punishment like a coiling snake.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the opposite opinion to step 17.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: They are one person; his real name was זמרי, and עכן describes the harm he caused.

steps.title: Back to the משנה: the man who cannot confess
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the next part of the משנה: a condemned man who does not know how to confess, and רבי יהודה's view.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'If he does not know how to confess, etc.' 'רבי יהודה says, etc.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves back to the משנה and quotes its next lines. It is setting up a question on the חכמים' words in that משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the משנה, a man who cannot confess says, 'Let my death atone for all my sins.' רבי יהודה says that if he knows he is innocent, he may say 'except for this sin.' The חכמים objected that then everyone would say that 'to clear themselves.'

keyTerms.meaning: Etc. (the quote continues in the משנה)

phrases.english: If he does not know how to confess, etc.
Rabbi Yehuda says, etc.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the עכן discussion and returns to the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A condemned man confesses; רבי יהודה lets him exclude the sin he says he did not do, and the חכמים reject this.

steps.title: So let them clear their names
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the חכמים: if people want to clear themselves, why not let them?
steps.simpleTranslation: 'To clear themselves.' So let them clear themselves!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the חכמים' worry and asks what is wrong with it. If a condemned man wants to proclaim his innocence, why should anyone stop him?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The חכמים treated 'everyone will clear themselves' as a bad result. The גמרא does not see the harm: a man about to die should be allowed to say he is innocent.

keyTerms.meaning: To clear themselves (of guilt in people's eyes)

phrases.english: "To clear themselves"
So let them clear themselves!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the reasoning of the חכמים quoted in step 19.
steps.kashyaTarget: The חכמים' objection to רבי יהודה in the משנה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Letting a condemned man clear his name seems harmless, so it is not a good reason to forbid his statement.

steps.title: To protect the courts and witnesses
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the statement would make people speak badly about the courts and the witnesses.
steps.simpleTranslation: So as not to spread a bad name about the courts and about the witnesses.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the harm: if every condemned man says he is innocent, people will start to think the courts and the witnesses are getting it wrong.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The problem is not the man himself but the damage to the court's reputation. Public trust in the courts and witnesses matters more than one man's chance to clear his name.

phrases.english: So as not to spread a bad name
about the courts and about the witnesses.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 20.
steps.terutzMaskana: It would damage the reputation of the courts and the witnesses.

steps.title: The man who declared his innocence on the way to execution
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא tells of a man going to his execution who said: if I did this sin, let my death not atone; if I did not, let it atone, the court is clear, and the witnesses will never be forgiven.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: A man was going out to be executed. He said: 'If I did this sin, let my death not atone for all my sins. If I did not do this sin, let my death atone for all my sins. The court and all ישראל are clear, and the witnesses will never be forgiven.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a story from a ברייתא about a condemned man who made a powerful statement of innocence. It is setting up the חכמים' reaction in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The man cleverly avoided blaming the court: he said the court and ישראל are clear, and he put all the blame on the witnesses. He also staked his own atonement on his claim, which made his words very believable.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
There was an incident with one person
who was going out to be executed.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר: אִם יֵשׁ בִּי עָוֹן זֶה,
phrases.english: He said: If I committed this sin,

phrases.aramaic: לֹא תְּהֵא מִיתָתִי כַּפָּרָה לְכׇל עֲוֹנוֹתַי.
phrases.english: let my death not be an atonement for all my sins.
But if I did not commit this sin,
let my death be an atonement for all my sins,
and the court and all of Israel are clear,

phrases.aramaic: וְהָעֵדִים לֹא תְּהֵא לָהֶם מְחִילָה לְעוֹלָם.
phrases.english: but the witnesses will never have forgiveness.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: מַעֲשֶׂה בְּאָדָם אֶחָד שֶׁיָּצָא לֵיהָרֵג
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a real case of a condemned man claiming innocence, the exact topic of steps 19-21.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A condemned man declared his innocence while clearing the court and blaming the witnesses.

steps.title: The חכמים rule: he is still executed
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים said they cannot bring him back since the sentence was already decided; he is executed, and the guilt hangs on the witnesses.
steps.simpleTranslation: When the חכמים heard this, they said: It is impossible to bring him back, since the decree was already decreed. Rather, he is executed, and the chain hangs on the witnesses' necks.
steps.whatsHappening: The חכמים respond to the man's statement. They rule that the sentence stays, and if he is truly innocent, the witnesses carry the guilt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His words do not reopen the case, because the court's verdict is final. Instead of undoing the ruling, the חכמים place the responsibility on the witnesses if they lied.

keyTerms.meaning: The decree was decreed (the verdict is final)
A chain or collar (here: the guilt)

phrases.english: And when the Sages heard about the matter, they said:
It is impossible to bring him back,
since the decree has already been decreed.
Rather, he shall be executed,
and the chain will hang on the necks of the witnesses.
phrases.notes: A picture-phrase: the blame for his death hangs on the witnesses like a chain around their necks.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the חכמים' ruling on the story in step 22.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A finished verdict is not undone by the condemned man's claim; the witnesses bear the guilt if they lied.

steps.title: Isn't that obvious?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the story is needed: of course a condemned man cannot cancel his sentence just by saying he is innocent.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is obvious! Is it in his power?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the point of the ברייתא. Obviously the man's own words cannot overturn a court ruling, so why teach it?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Every condemned man would like to say he is innocent. If his word alone could stop the execution, no one would ever be executed, so the ruling seems too obvious to need a story.

phrases.english: It is obvious!
Is it in his power [to cancel the sentence]?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions why the ruling in step 23 needed to be taught.
steps.kashyaTarget: The חכמים' ruling in the ברייתא
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A condemned man's own claim obviously cannot override the verdict, so the ruling teaches nothing new.

steps.title: Even when the witnesses take back their testimony
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the story teaches he is executed even when the witnesses retracted.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it is needed for a case where the witnesses retracted.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the new lesson by reading the story as a case where the witnesses themselves took back what they said, and still the execution went ahead.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If only the condemned man spoke, the ruling would be obvious. The חידוש is that even the witnesses' own retraction does not undo a final verdict, since 'the decree was already decreed.'

keyTerms.meaning: No, it is needed (for a special case)

steps.whatToRemember: Once the court has ruled, the sentence stands even if the witnesses take back their testimony; the guilt rests on them.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't think the story only teaches that the condemned man cannot save himself; that part is obvious. This step says the new point is about the witnesses retracting, and Step 27 sharpens that point further.

phrases.english: No, it is necessary
where the witnesses retracted their testimony.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא צְרִיכָא דְּקָא הָדְרִי בְּהוּ סָהֲדִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 24 by narrowing the case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The story only teaches that the condemned man's claim does not help, which is obvious.
steps.terutzMaskana: The story teaches that even the witnesses' retraction does not overturn the final verdict.

steps.title: Why does it matter if the witnesses take back their words?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the answer from Step 25. A witness can never take back testimony, so it is obvious that the man is still executed.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if the witnesses took back their words, so what? Once a witness has testified, he cannot go back and testify differently!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the answer it just gave in Step 25. It says that a story about witnesses taking back their testimony teaches nothing new.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 25 said the story teaches that the man is executed even though the witnesses took back their testimony. But there is a fixed rule: once a witness testifies, he cannot change his testimony. So their taking it back means nothing, and we already knew the man would be executed.

keyTerms.meaning: They went back on their words (took back their testimony)
So what? What difference does it make?

keyTerms.term: כֵּיוָן שֶׁהִגִּיד שׁוּב אֵינוֹ חוֹזֵר וּמַגִּיד
keyTerms.meaning: Once a witness has testified, he cannot go back and testify differently

steps.confusionAlert: Don't think the גמרא is asking whether the man should be freed. Both sides agree he is executed. The question is only why the story needed to teach something that seems obvious.

phrases.english: And if they took back their words,
what of it?
Once he has testified,
he cannot go back and testify again!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer given in Step 25
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer in Step 25 that the story teaches execution even after the witnesses retract
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A witness's retraction has no legal power anyway (כיון שהגיד אינו חוזר ומגיד), so the story would be teaching nothing new.

steps.title: Even when the witnesses give a reason for their lie
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the story teaches the man is executed even when the witnesses explain why they lied, like the story of בעיא the tax collector.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, the story is needed for a case where the witnesses even give a reason for what they said, like that incident of בעיא the tax collector.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends its answer. It narrows the case so the story does teach something new.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A plain retraction obviously means nothing. But here the witnesses give a believable reason for having lied, which might make us think we should listen to them. The story teaches that even then, the verdict stands and the man is executed.

keyTerms.meaning: It is needed only for this case (introduces a narrower case)
They give a reason for what they said
בעיא the tax collector, a well-known story

steps.whatToRemember: Once witnesses have testified and the sentence is decided, their taking it back does not stop the execution, even if they explain why they lied.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows how firm the rule כיון שהגיד אינו חוזר ומגיד is. Even a convincing explanation does not let a witness undo his testimony.

phrases.english: No, it is needed
for when, even though
they give a reason for their words,
like that incident
of Ba'aya the tax collector.
phrases.notes: The גמרא only names this story here. It is a known case where witnesses had a hidden reason to lie.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא צְרִיכָא, דְּאַף עַל גַּב דְּקָא יָהֲבִי טַעְמָא לְמִילְּתַיְיהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 26
steps.terutzHavaAmina: When witnesses give a convincing reason for having lied, we might believe their retraction and stop the execution.
steps.terutzMaskana: Even with a reason given, the retraction is ignored and the man is executed.

steps.title: Removing the clothes and רבי יהודה's view on covering
steps.stepSummary: The new משנה teaches that four אמות from the place of stoning, the clothes are taken off. רבי יהודה says a man is covered in front and a woman in front and back.
steps.simpleTranslation: When he was four אמות from the place of stoning, they take off his clothes. A man is covered in front, and a woman in front and in back. These are the words of רבי יהודה.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It describes the next stage of the stoning and gives רבי יהודה's opinion on how to cover the person.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The procedure moves forward: close to the place of stoning, the clothes are removed. רבי יהודה says a man still gets a front covering, and a woman gets covering both in front and in back.

keyTerms.meaning: Our משנה (start of a new משנה)

phrases.english: MISHNA:
When he was away from the place of stoning
four cubits,
they take off his clothes.
A man, they cover him in front,
and a woman, in front and in back,
these are the words of Rabbi Yehuda.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָיָה רָחוֹק מִבֵּית הַסְּקִילָה אַרְבַּע אַמּוֹת, מַפְשִׁיטִין אוֹתוֹ אֶת בְּגָדָיו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה continuing the order of the stoning procedure
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Four אמות from the place of stoning the clothes are removed; according to רבי יהודה a man is covered in front and a woman in front and back.

steps.title: The חכמים: a man without clothes, a woman clothed
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים disagree with רבי יהודה. A man is stoned without his clothes, but a woman is not stoned without clothes.
steps.simpleTranslation: But the חכמים say: a man is stoned without clothes, and a woman is not stoned without clothes.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives the חכמים's opinion, which disagrees with רבי יהודה about the woman.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For a man, the חכמים say he is stoned without his clothes, keeping only the front covering. For a woman they disagree with רבי יהודה: she keeps her clothes on and is not stripped at all.

keyTerms.meaning: But the חכמים say (the majority view)

steps.confusionAlert: "Without clothes" for the man does not mean fully uncovered. He still keeps a cloth covering in front; the dispute is mainly about the woman.

phrases.english: But the Rabbis say:
A man is stoned without clothes,
phrases.notes: He still keeps a small cloth covering in front, just not his regular clothes.

phrases.english: and a woman is not stoned without clothes.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the opposing view to רבי יהודה in the same משנה
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A man is stoned without his clothes; a woman is stoned clothed.
